units.subject: Biology
units.title: Aquatic Habitat
objectives: Define aquatic habitat and distinguish freshwater from marine environments.
Explain how light, temperature, salinity, depth and dissolved oxygen affect aquatic organisms.
units.body:
Aquatic Habitat

Aquatic habitats include freshwater rivers, streams, lakes and ponds, and marine seas and oceans. Estuaries form where fresh river water mixes with seawater, so salinity changes with tides and rainfall. Light decreases with depth and limits photosynthesis; temperature affects metabolism and oxygen availability; dissolved oxygen supports aerobic respiration; salinity affects water balance. Currents, waves, pressure, turbidity and the nature of the bottom also shape the organisms that can live there. Plankton drift with water, nekton swim actively, and benthos live on or in the bottom. Phytoplankton are producers, while zooplankton commonly feed on other plankton. Habitat protection requires water-quality control, wetland protection and sustainable fishing.

Applying the concept: identify the environmental condition or biological process first, then explain how it affects an organism or ecosystem. Use a cause-and-effect sequence rather than naming terms without explanation. In a local example, state the habitat or process, identify the relevant factor, describe the biological response and explain the likely ecological consequence. Where several factors interact, avoid claiming that one factor alone caused an observed change without evidence.

Key learning check: define the main term accurately; distinguish related concepts; give a relevant example; and explain the relationship between structure, function and environment. The examples in this lesson are original teaching illustrations, not quotations from the supplied school document. The source audit records the corresponding scheme topic and body-section anchor.

units.title: Terrestrial Habitat
objectives: Define terrestrial habitat and identify major abiotic factors.
Compare rainforest, savanna, desert and grassland habitats.
units.body:
Terrestrial Habitat

A terrestrial habitat is a land environment occupied by organisms. Climate, soil, relief and water availability influence the vegetation and animals found there. Tropical rainforests generally have high rainfall and layered vegetation. Savannas have grasses with scattered trees and often distinct wet and dry seasons. Deserts receive little rainfall, so organisms face water shortage and sometimes large daily temperature changes. Grasslands are dominated by grasses where rainfall, fire, grazing or soil conditions restrict tree cover. Rainfall, temperature, soil texture, pH, nutrients, light and wind are abiotic factors; competition, grazing, predation and mutualism are biotic factors. Organisms show features that help them function in local conditions, such as water-storing tissues, deep roots, burrowing behaviour or seasonal dormancy.

Applying the concept: identify the environmental condition or biological process first, then explain how it affects an organism or ecosystem. Use a cause-and-effect sequence rather than naming terms without explanation. In a local example, state the habitat or process, identify the relevant factor, describe the biological response and explain the likely ecological consequence. Where several factors interact, avoid claiming that one factor alone caused an observed change without evidence.

Key learning check: define the main term accurately; distinguish related concepts; give a relevant example; and explain the relationship between structure, function and environment. The examples in this lesson are original teaching illustrations, not quotations from the supplied school document. The source audit records the corresponding scheme topic and body-section anchor.

units.subject: Biology
units.title: Food Production and Storage
objectives: Explain the roles of producers, consumers and decomposers.
Describe food chains and food webs and explain common food preservation methods.
units.body:
Food Production and Storage

Food production depends on ecological processes. Green plants and algae are producers: they use light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into organic substances during photosynthesis. Consumers obtain energy by feeding on plants or other organisms. Decomposers, especially bacteria and fungi, break down dead material and wastes, returning nutrients to the environment. A food chain shows one feeding pathway; a food web combines connected chains. Energy is transferred between trophic levels, but some is used in life processes and dissipated as heat. Food preservation slows microorganisms and enzymes: drying removes available water, refrigeration slows microbial growth, freezing slows it further, salting and sugaring reduce water availability, and canning combines heat treatment with an airtight container. Safe storage also requires clean handling, suitable containers and pest control.

units.title: Nutrient Cycling in Nature
objectives: Explain why matter is recycled while energy flows through ecosystems.
Describe the water and carbon cycles.
units.body:
Nutrient Cycling in Nature

Nutrient cycling is the movement and reuse of elements between organisms and the non-living environment. Organisms need carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and other elements to build cells. Energy, in contrast, enters ecosystems mainly as sunlight and is eventually dissipated as heat. The water cycle includes evaporation from water and soil, transpiration from plants, condensation into clouds, precipitation, runoff and infiltration into the ground. Organisms also take up and return water through life processes. Carbon enters organic matter when plants and algae take in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis. It passes to consumers through feeding and returns to the environment through respiration, decomposition and combustion. These cycles connect living organisms with the atmosphere, soil and water.

units.title: Nutrient Cycling in Nature (Continued)

units.body:
Nutrient Cycling in Nature (Continued)

Nitrogen is needed to make amino acids, proteins and nucleic acids. Although atmospheric nitrogen gas is abundant, most plants cannot use it directly. Nitrogen fixation converts nitrogen gas into ammonia or related compounds and is carried out by certain microorganisms, including bacteria associated with legume root nodules. Nitrification converts ammonium to nitrite and then nitrate. Plants assimilate ammonium or nitrate into organic compounds; animals obtain nitrogen by feeding. Decomposers break down wastes and dead organisms, and ammonification releases ammonia or ammonium. Under suitable conditions, denitrifying bacteria convert nitrate to gaseous nitrogen forms that return to the atmosphere. Excess fertiliser can leach or run off into water, stimulate algal blooms and contribute to oxygen depletion when algae die and decompose.

units.title: Pollution
objectives: Define pollution and distinguish major forms of pollution.

units.body:
Pollution

Pollution is the introduction of substances or forms of energy into the environment at levels or places that cause harm. Air pollution may come from vehicle exhaust, generators, industrial emissions and open burning. Water pollution may result from sewage, oil spills, industrial discharge, fertiliser runoff and plastics. Soil pollution can follow poor waste management, excessive pesticide use and chemical leakage. Noise from traffic and machinery can interfere with communication and sleep; thermal pollution changes habitat temperature. Nutrient pollution can cause eutrophication, while pathogens in contaminated water can spread disease. Some persistent pollutants accumulate in organisms and certain substances may biomagnify through food chains. Control begins with prevention: treat sewage, manage industrial effluent, reduce waste, handle farm chemicals responsibly and prevent dumping into drains and waterways.

units.title: Conservation of Natural Resources
objectives: Distinguish renewable and non-renewable resources.
Compare in-situ and ex-situ conservation and explain sustainable resource use.
units.body:
Conservation of Natural Resources

Natural resources include water, soil, forests, wildlife, fish, minerals, sunlight and fossil fuels. Renewable resources can be replenished by natural processes, but may still be depleted if used faster than they recover. Non-renewable resources such as many mineral deposits and fossil fuels form over geological timescales. Conservation protects, restores and uses resources sustainably. Biodiversity includes variation within species, between species and among ecosystems. Ecosystems provide food, clean water, pollination, soil formation and nutrient cycling. In-situ conservation protects organisms in their natural habitats, for example in national parks and forest reserves. Ex-situ conservation protects them outside those habitats, for example in seed banks, botanical gardens and zoos. Reforestation, controlled harvesting, soil conservation and wetland protection support sustainable use.

units.body:
Ecological Management and Tolerance

Every organism can survive and reproduce only within a range of environmental conditions. A range of tolerance is the interval between the minimum and maximum levels of a factor that an organism can endure. Factors include temperature, salinity, pH, moisture, light, oxygen and nutrient availability. Within the range, performance is often greatest near an optimum. Conditions farther from the optimum may create stress and reduce growth, feeding or reproduction. Beyond the limits, the organism cannot survive for long. A limiting factor can restrict distribution even when other conditions are suitable. Ecological management applies this knowledge: fish ponds need suitable oxygen and temperature; riverbank vegetation can reduce erosion; soil testing and appropriate irrigation can help avoid salinity or waterlogging. Monitoring is needed because several factors may act together.

units.title: Adaptation
objectives: Define adaptation and distinguish structural, physiological and behavioural adaptations.
Explain how inherited variation and natural selection change populations over generations.
units.body:
Adaptation

An adaptation is an inherited feature that, in a particular environment, contributes to survival and reproduction. Structural adaptations are physical features, such as streamlined bodies or thick waxy leaf cuticles. Physiological adaptations are functional processes, such as producing concentrated urine to conserve water. Behavioural adaptations are activities, such as nocturnal feeding that reduces exposure to daytime heat. Populations contain inherited variation. When individuals with particular inherited variants leave more offspring in a given environment, those variants may become more common over generations through natural selection. Individuals do not acquire a useful inherited feature simply because they need it. Aquatic examples include gills and osmoregulatory mechanisms; terrestrial examples include deep roots, water-resistant coverings and burrowing behaviour. units.title: Tissue and Supporting System (Continued)
objectives: Identify the four primary animal tissue types and relate their structures to functions.
Explain how skeletons and supporting tissues provide shape, protection and movement.
units.body:
Tissue and Supporting System (Continued)

Multicellular animals are organised from cells into tissues, organs and organ systems. The four primary animal tissue groups are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue. Epithelial tissue covers body surfaces and lines cavities; connective tissue supports, binds and protects; muscle tissue contracts to produce movement; nervous tissue detects and transmits signals. Different tissues combine within an organ, so an organ performs functions that no single tissue could perform alone. Supporting systems include the skeleton and connective tissues. Bone is a hard, mineralised connective tissue that supports and protects; cartilage is more flexible and cushions joints. A skeleton may be internal, external or hydrostatic. Muscles act on supporting structures to move the body, while joints permit movement between bones.

Learning application: identify the relevant structure, process or environmental factor, then explain its function and the consequence of a change. Use correct biological terms and show the sequence of events where a process is involved. Compare related terms explicitly rather than treating them as synonyms. Examples in this lesson are original teaching illustrations informed by the cited references; they are not quotations from the school source or from the external text.

Check your understanding by defining the central terms, labelling relevant structures, tracing the process in the correct order and applying the explanation to a familiar organism or situation. A strong answer names the structure or process, states its function and explains how that function contributes to the organism or ecosystem.

units.title: Mammalian Teeth
objectives: Identify the main types of mammalian teeth and their functions.
Describe the basic structure of a tooth and relate dentition to diet.
units.body:
Mammalian Teeth

Mammalian teeth are specialised structures used to obtain and process food. Many mammals have different types of teeth, a condition called heterodont dentition. Incisors cut or bite, canines pierce or tear, premolars crush and grind, and molars grind food. The relative development of each type is related to feeding habits, although tooth patterns vary among species. A typical tooth has a crown above the gum, a neck near the gum line and a root anchored in the jaw. Enamel covers the crown and is highly mineralised; dentine forms much of the tooth; the pulp cavity contains nerves and blood vessels. Cementum helps attach the root through periodontal tissues. Good oral hygiene reduces plaque accumulation and the risk of tooth decay and gum disease.

Digestive System (Continued)

The digestive system changes food into small molecules that can be absorbed and used by cells. Ingestion is taking in food. Mechanical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces, while chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into smaller soluble products. Food passes through the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum and anus. Saliva begins starch digestion; the stomach churns food and provides an acidic environment for protein digestion; the small intestine receives bile and pancreatic juice and is the main site of digestion and absorption. Villi and microvilli increase the absorptive surface. The liver produces bile, the gall bladder stores it, and the pancreas releases digestive enzymes and bicarbonate. The large intestine absorbs water and forms faeces. Egestion is removal of undigested material, not the same as excretion.

Transport System

Transport systems move useful substances to cells and carry wastes away. Small organisms may exchange materials by diffusion over short distances, but diffusion alone is too slow for the needs of large multicellular bodies. In many animals, a circulatory system includes a pumping organ, a transport fluid and vessels or spaces through which the fluid moves. Blood carries oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, hormones, heat and metabolic wastes. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins return blood to the heart, and capillaries have thin walls that allow exchange with tissues. A closed circulatory system keeps blood within vessels; an open system allows circulating fluid to bathe organs directly. Transport is coordinated with digestion, respiration and excretion.

objectives: Describe the structure and function of the mammalian heart.

units.body:
Circulatory System

The mammalian circulatory system is closed and has double circulation. The heart has four chambers: right and left atria receive blood, while right and left ventricles pump blood out. The right side sends oxygen-poor blood to the lungs for gas exchange; the left side sends oxygen-rich blood to the body. Valves help prevent backflow. Pulmonary circulation is the route between heart and lungs, while systemic circulation is the route between heart and body tissues. Arteries have relatively thick, elastic walls to withstand higher pressure; veins have thinner walls and often contain valves; capillaries have very thin walls for exchange. Blood contains plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Red cells transport oxygen using haemoglobin; white cells defend against pathogens; platelets help blood clot.

objectives: Describe the functions of xylem and phloem.

units.body:
Transport System in Higher Plants

Plants transport water, mineral ions and organic products between roots, stems and leaves. Xylem vessels and tracheids conduct water and dissolved mineral ions mainly from roots towards the leaves; their thickened walls also provide support. Water enters root cells from the soil by osmosis and moves towards the xylem. Evaporation of water from leaf surfaces through stomata creates a transpiration pull that helps draw water up the plant. Phloem transports sugars and other organic solutes from sources, such as photosynthesising leaves, to sinks, such as growing roots, fruits and storage organs. This movement is called translocation and can occur in different directions in different sieve tubes. Transpiration is water loss, whereas translocation is movement of organic solutes.

Respiratory System

The respiratory system brings oxygen into the body and removes carbon dioxide. In mammals, air passes through the nose or mouth, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles before reaching the alveoli in the lungs. Gas exchange occurs across the thin walls of alveoli and surrounding capillaries. Oxygen diffuses from air in the alveoli into the blood, while carbon dioxide diffuses from blood into the alveolar air. Alveoli provide a large surface area, have moist surfaces, thin walls and a rich blood supply. Ventilation continually refreshes the air and helps maintain concentration gradients. The respiratory system works with the circulatory system: blood transports oxygen to tissues and carries carbon dioxide back to the lungs.

Respiratory System (Continued)

Breathing, or ventilation, moves air into and out of the lungs. During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the external intercostal muscles lift the ribs. The thoracic cavity volume increases, pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure and air moves in. During quiet exhalation, these muscles relax, thoracic volume decreases, pressure rises and air moves out. Gas exchange is diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide across respiratory surfaces, such as alveoli. Cellular respiration is the series of chemical reactions in cells that releases usable energy from food molecules; it is not the same as breathing. Oxygen is carried mainly by haemoglobin, while carbon dioxide is transported in several forms, especially as bicarbonate ions in blood.

Excretion in Lower Organisms

Excretion is the removal of metabolic waste products from an organism. It must be distinguished from egestion, which is the removal of undigested food. Very small organisms may remove soluble wastes by diffusion across the cell surface. Many freshwater protozoans use contractile vacuoles to collect and expel excess water, helping maintain osmotic balance. Flatworms such as planarians have flame-cell systems that move fluid and wastes through tubules. Earthworms use nephridia to filter body fluid and regulate water and salts. Insects commonly use Malpighian tubules, which transfer nitrogenous wastes from body fluid into the gut for removal. These structures differ, but each helps remove wastes and maintain a suitable internal environment.

units.body:
Excretory System in Vertebrates and Plants

Vertebrate kidneys help remove nitrogenous wastes and regulate water and dissolved salts. In mammals, each kidney contains many nephrons. Blood is filtered at the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule. Useful substances and much of the water are reabsorbed along the renal tubule, while selected substances are secreted into the tubule. The remaining fluid becomes urine and passes through the ureter to the bladder and then the urethra. The kidney therefore contributes to osmoregulation as well as excretion. Plants do not have kidneys or a single specialised excretory organ. They may release gases through stomata and lenticels, store some wastes in vacuoles or tissues, accumulate substances in leaves or bark that are later shed, and produce resins, gums or latex.

units.title: Male and Female Reproductive Structures; Sexual Reproduction
objectives: Identify the main male and female reproductive structures in mammals.
Explain gamete formation, fertilisation and early development.
units.body:
Male and Female Reproductive Structures; Sexual Reproduction

Sexual reproduction involves the formation and fusion of male and female gametes. In mammals, the testes produce sperm and testosterone; sperm mature and are transported through ducts before leaving through the urethra. The ovaries produce ova and reproductive hormones. An ovum released during ovulation may enter an oviduct, where fertilisation can occur if sperm are present. The uterus supports development of an embryo and foetus during pregnancy, while the cervix and vagina form parts of the reproductive tract. Gametes are produced by meiosis, which halves the chromosome number. Fertilisation restores the diploid number when the nuclei of sperm and ovum unite to form a zygote. The zygote divides by mitosis and develops through early embryonic stages.

objectives: Identify the reproductive parts of a typical flowering plant.

units.body:
Reproduction in Plants

A typical flower contains male and female reproductive structures. The stamen consists of an anther, where pollen is produced, and a filament. The carpel or pistil includes stigma, style and ovary; ovules are contained in the ovary. Pollen carries the male gametophyte. After a compatible pollen grain reaches the stigma, it may germinate and grow a pollen tube through the style towards an ovule. In flowering plants, fertilisation involves male gametes delivered by the pollen tube; one fuses with the egg to form a zygote and another participates in forming endosperm. After fertilisation, the ovule develops into a seed and the ovary commonly develops into a fruit. Some plants also reproduce asexually through runners, bulbs, tubers or cuttings.

objectives: Define pollination and distinguish self-pollination from cross-pollination.

units.body:
Pollination

Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma. Self-pollination occurs when pollen reaches the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant. Cross-pollination occurs when pollen is transferred to a flower on a different plant of the same species. Wind-pollinated flowers often produce abundant light pollen and may have exposed anthers and feathery stigmas. Animal-pollinated flowers often have colour, scent, nectar and pollen that attract visitors. Water pollination occurs in some aquatic plants. Pollination is not fertilisation: pollination places pollen on the stigma, while fertilisation occurs later when male and female gametes fuse in the ovule. Cross-pollination can increase genetic variation among offspring.

units.title: Ecological Succession
objectives: Define ecological succession and distinguish primary from secondary succession.

units.body:
Ecological Succession

Ecological succession is the gradual change in the species composition and structure of a community over time. Primary succession begins on a surface where soil is absent or extremely limited, such as newly exposed rock. Pioneer organisms, including lichens and some mosses, help weather rock and contribute organic matter as they grow and die. Soil develops gradually, allowing grasses, shrubs and later larger plants to establish where climate and other conditions permit. Secondary succession occurs where a community has been disturbed but soil remains, for example after a fire or abandoned cultivation. It is often faster because seeds, roots, microorganisms and soil nutrients may remain. Succession is not always a simple fixed sequence ending in one permanent climax community; disturbance and environmental conditions can alter its course.

objectives: Explain how population density can affect competition for resources.

units.body:
Overcrowding and Food Shortage

Population density is the number of individuals of a species in a given area or volume. When a population becomes large relative to available food, water, space and shelter, individuals may compete more strongly. Competition can reduce growth, reproduction and survival. Carrying capacity is the population size that an environment can support over time under prevailing conditions; it can change when resources or environmental conditions change. Density-dependent factors, such as competition, disease and parasitism, often have stronger effects as population density rises. Density-independent factors, such as drought, floods or severe storms, can affect populations regardless of their density. Food shortage can lead to migration, reduced reproduction, starvation or changes in predator-prey relationships.

units.title: Balance in Nature; Family Planning
objectives: Explain how interactions among organisms and environmental factors contribute to ecological balance.

units.body:
Balance in Nature; Family Planning

Ecological balance describes a condition in which populations and environmental processes interact without one change causing uncontrolled disruption to the whole system. Food webs, competition, predation, decomposition, nutrient cycling and habitat conditions all contribute. Balance does not mean that populations never change; natural systems fluctuate with seasons, resources and disturbance. Excessive harvesting, pollution, habitat destruction and invasive species can disrupt relationships and reduce resilience. Family planning is a human reproductive-health topic: it concerns informed and voluntary decisions about whether and when to have children and the spacing of pregnancies. Methods include barrier, hormonal, intrauterine, fertility-awareness and permanent methods. The suitability of a method depends on health and individual circumstances and should be discussed with a qualified health worker. Condoms are the only contraceptive method that also helps protect against sexually transmitted infections, including HIV. No learner should be pressured to disclose personal or family circumstances during classroom activities.
